records.text: brain tumor diagnosis and classification remain critical challenges in modern healthcare. recent advancements in artificial intelligence ( ai ), particularly deep learning ( dl ) and machine learning ( ml ), have significantly enhanced medical image analysis, enabling automated and accurate detection of brain tumors. this paper reviews a wide range of ml and dl approaches for brain tumor detection, including convolutional neural networks ( cnns ), recurrent neural networks ( rnns ), generative adversarial networks ( gans ), hybrid architectures, vision transformers ( vits ), transfer learning ( tl ), attention mechanisms, and ensemble learning methods. also, ai applications are highlighted across different medical imaging modalities, summarize commonly used publicly available datasets, and discuss preprocessing techniques adopted in recent studies. furthermore, the paper addresses evaluation metrics, compares state - of - the - art dl approaches, and examines key challenges and limitations. finally, future research directions are proposed to guide the development of more robust and clinically effective ai - based solutions. this review aims to provide researchers and clinicians with a comprehensive understanding of ais potential in advancing brain tumor diagnosis and detection.

records.text: brain tumors are abnormal growths of cells in the brain, which can be benign or malignant. thus, brain tumors represent one of the most critical and life - threatening medical conditions, with approximately 300, 000 new cases diagnosed globally each year [ 1 ]. accurate and early classification and detection are essential for effective treatment planning, improving patient outcomes, prognosis prediction, patient management, and patient survival. traditional diagnostic methods, such as biopsy and manual analysis, are clinicians in brain tumor classification [ 6 ]. these techniques have demonstrated remarkable potential for non - invasive brain tumor classification utilizing medical imaging data. the application of ai in this domain has evolved rapidly, transitioning from traditional ml approaches to sophisticated dl architectures. these computational methods are used to analyse data of medical imaging to detect patterns and features beyond the capabilities of the human visual system, potentially improving diagnostic accuracy and efficiency [ 7 ]. time consuming, and potentially invasive [ 2 ]. often, these traditional diagnosis methods require expert radiological assessment followed by histopathological examination and rely on medical imaging techniques [ 3 ].

in recent years, the integration of machine learning ( ml ) and deep learning ( dl ) techniques into medical imaging has demonstrated considerable success in enhancing diagnostic precision and workflow efficiency, particularly in brain tumor detection and classification. so, these techniques are a powerful tool for automating brain tumor classification, improving accuracy, and reducing diagnostic delays. brain tumors are broadly classified as primary ( originating in the brain ) or metastatic ( spreading from other parts of the body ). primary brain tumors are further classified according to the world health organization ( who ) classification system, which categorizes brain tumors into four grades based on their cell of origin and malignancy grade ( i - iv ) [ 4 ], with each grade requiring distinct treatment approaches. grade iv represents the most aggressive form, such as glioblastoma multiforme ( gbm ). the normal cerebrospinal fluid ( csf ) system in the brain is shown in fig. 1. this figure demonstrates different parts of the brain, especially a particular tumor region [ 5 ]. over the past decade, ai approaches - particularly ml and dl - have emerged as promising tools to assist however, manual interpretation of medical images presents several challenges, including inter - observer variability, the time - consuming nature of the process, and potential for human error due to the complex and heterogeneous appearance of brain tumors [ 8 ]. these limitations have motivated the development of computer aided diagnosis ( cad ) systems to help clinicians in the detection and classification of brain tumors. in recent years, dl approaches have emerged as powerful tools for medical image analysis, demonstrating remarkable success in tasks such as tumor detection, segmentation, and classification [ 9 ].

regarding dl, it is a subset of ml, employs neural networks with multiple layers to learn hierarchical representations from data. unlike traditional ml approaches that require hand - crafted features, dl models can capture relevant features, making them particularly suitable for complex pattern recognition tasks in medical imaging [ 10 ]. the application of dl to brain tumor analysis has witnessed significant advancements, with various architectures being proposed to address different aspects of the problem. brain tumors are classified according to the who, which categorizes tumors based on histopathological features and molecular markers [ 4 ]. these types of brain tumors include gliomas, meningiomas, schwannomas, pituitary adenomas, medulloblastomas, and metastatic tumors. gliomas arise from glial cells, which are further classified into grades i - iv based on malignancy. meningiomas typically represent benign tumors originating in the meninges. pituitary adenomas develop in the pituitary gland, while schwannomas form on the schwann cells that cover cranial nerves. benign tumors develop on the vestibulocochlear nerve. medulloblastomas primarily occur in the cerebellum, most common in children. metastatic tumors are cancers that spread to the brain from other body parts. fig. 2 illustrates different types of brain tumors. commonly utilized neuroimaging modalities include magnetic resonance imaging ( mri ), which delivers detailed structural information useful for detecting brain atrophy ; records.text: in the field of brain tumor classification, it ' s vital to evaluate dl models carefully to ensure they are both accurate and applicable in a clinical context. various metrics are used to variants include t1, t2, flair, and contrast - enhanced images. ct scans, pet scans, and histopathological slides have also been used for multimodal classification tasks, enhancing diagnostic accuracy through data fusion. computed tomography ( ct ) is an advanced medical imaging method that uses x - ray technology to generate cross - sectional images of the body ' s internal structure. during the procedure, the patient lies inside a rotating scanner, where x - rays collect data from multiple angles. this data is then processed by a computer to create 2d images for diagnostic purposes. the ct offers rapid acquisition and good visualization of bone, calcification, and hemorrhage. ct scans are widely utilized to identify tumors and internal bleeding, making them especially valuable in emergency situations because of their rapid imaging capabilities. they provide high - resolution images of both bone and soft tissues ; however, they expose patients to ionizing radiation and generally offer less detailed soft tissue contrast compared to mri scans [ 81 ]. structural magnetic resonance imaging ( smri ) is a non - invasive imaging method that uses powerful magnetic fields to generate high - resolution images of internal body structures. it is especially effective to visualize brain anatomy and detect abnormalities such as tissue atrophy. smri is crucial for examining structural changes in neurodegenerative conditions like brain tumors. it offers exceptional soft tissue contrast without the risks of ionizing radiation. however, the procedure can be time - consuming, costly, and is not suitable for patients with metal implants or severe claustrophobia [ 82 ].

is a specialized type of mri that tracks the movement of water molecules within tissues, mainly to map neural pathways in the brain. by analyzing the direction of water diffusion, dti visualizes white matter tracts and brain connectivity. this technique is especially valuable for diagnosing conditions such brain stroke, and for studying neural disorders. the dti is a non invasive method that effectively assesses the integrity of white matter, though it is very sensitive to a motion artifact and involves complex data processing [ 84 ]. functional magnetic resonance imaging ( fmri ) assesses brain activity by tracking blood flow changes that occur in response to neural activation [ 85 ]. functional mri ( fmri ) leverages the blood oxygen level - dependent signal to identify regions of active brain within a particular problem. it is a crucial tool in cognitive neuroscience for mapping functions such as sensory regions, and plays an important role in pre surgical planning to remove brain tumor. although fmri is non - invasive and provides high spatial resolution, it measures neuronal activity indirectly through changes in blood flow and is highly susceptible to motion artifacts. mri provides excellent soft tissue contrast and is available in multiple sequences. these mri sequences commonly used in brain tumor imaging include : t1 - weighted : provides good anatomical detail ; tumors typically appear hypointense ( darker ). t1 - weighted with contrast enhancement ( t1ce ) : after gadolinium injection, areas with compromised blood - brain barrier ( e. g., active tumor regions ) appear hyperintense ( brighter ). t2 - weighted : shows edema well ; tumors and surrounding edema typically appear hyperintense. fluid attenuated inversion recovery ( flair ) : suppresses cerebrospinal fluid signal, highlighting edema associated with tumors. other imaging modalities like diffusion - weighted imaging ( dwi ), which measures water molecule diffusion, perfusion imaging, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy ( mrs ), which provide additional functional and metabolic information. figure 10 depicts the utilization percentages of various imaging modalities in brain tumors.

accuracy is one of the fundamental and widely used metrics in classification problems. it measures the proportion of total correct predictions ( including both positive and negative classes ) out of all instances. in the context of brain tumor classification, accuracy tells us how often the model correctly identifies both brain tumor patients and healthy subjects. eq. ( 1 ) illustrates the formula for calculating accuracy [ 90 ]. here, tp stands for true positives ( brain tumor cases correctly identified ), tn refers to true negatives ( healthy cases correctly classified ), fp denotes false positives ( healthy cases incorrectly predicted as brain tumor ), and fn indicates false negatives ( brain tumor cases incorrectly predicted as healthy ). although accuracy is a useful measure, it can sometimes provide a distorted picture, especially when the dataset is imbalanced and contains significantly more healthy individuals than brain tumor patients.

in medical classification tasks such as brain tumor detection, where the impact of false positives ( fps ) and false negatives ( fns ) can be critical, metrics like precision, recall, and the f1 - score are often favored over simple accuracy. precision, also known as positive predictive value ( ppv ), measures the proportion of true positive cases among all cases that the model predicted as positive. this is particularly important when false positives ( where healthy individuals are incorrectly diagnosed as having a brain tumor ) are a significant dsc = 2 × t p ( 2 × t p ) + ( f p + f n ) ( 8 )

recall, also referred to as sensitivity, measures the proportion of actual positive cases that a model correctly identifies. this metric is especially crucial in situations where missing true positive cases ( false negatives ) can have serious consequences, such as failing to detect brain tumor patients. eq. ( 3 ) demonstrates how recall is calculated [ 92 ].

the f1 - score represents the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing the two metrics to provide a comprehensive measure of the model ' s performance. this score is particularly valuable in cases of unbalanced datasets, offering a more balanced evaluation of a model ' s effectiveness than relying on accuracy alone. in brain tumor detection studies, the f1 - score is often prioritized because missing true positive cases ( false negatives ) poses a greater risk than misclassifying healthy individuals. the f1 - score is calculated using eq. records.text: the matthews correlation coefficient ( mcc ) is another valuable metric to assess binary classification models, particularly when working with unbalanced data. unlike accuracy, which can be misleading in such situations, mcc incorporates all four elements of the confusion matrix ( tp, tn, fp, fn ) to provide a comprehensive, balanced measure of model performance. mcc ranges from - 1 ( completely incorrect predictions ) to + 1 ( perfect predictions ), with a score of 0 indicating no better than random guessing. it ' s especially relevant when both classes hold similar importance. eq. ( 7 ) presents the formula for the mcc [ 96 ].

although not a standalone metric, the confusion matrix is an essential tool to visualize a model ' s performance. it shows the number of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives in a tabular form, making it easy to calculate various other metrics such as accuracy, recall, recall, and f1 - score. table 5 presents the confusion matrix values. this matrix is particularly useful for understanding how well the model distinguishes between the two classes and for pinpointing where it may be making mistakes. such insights are crucial in medical applications, where errors in prediction can have serious consequences.

the dice score coefficient ( dsc ) is a widely used evaluation metric that measures the degree of overlap between the predicted segmentation and the actual ground truth. it assesses similarity by comparing the number of true positives relative to the average size of the predicted and actual regions. mathematically, it is expressed in eq. ( 8 ) [ 97 ].

loss is commonly used to evaluate classification models that produce probability estimates instead of fixed class labels. this metric measures how well the predicted probabilities align with the actual outcomes, imposing a greater penalty when the model confidently makes incorrect predictions. the formula for log loss is demonstrated in eq. ( 9 ) [ 98 ]. here, y i represents the true label of the i th instance either ( 0 or 1 ), yi denotes the predicted probability for the same instance, and n is the total number of instances in the dataset. lower loss values indicate better model performance, with a perfect prediction achieving a log loss of zero. each of these evaluation metrics offers unique benefits depending on the specific challenges of brain tumor classification. while accuracy gives a broad overview of how well the model performs, metrics such as precision and mcc provide a more nuanced evaluation, especially when dealing with imbalanced datasets. additionally, confusion matrices and log loss deepen the analysis by revealing the types of errors the model makes. a thorough understanding of these metrics is essential for developing dl models that are not only accurate but also dependable and safe for clinical use.

error analysis plays a vital role in assessing ai models, particularly in critical domains like healthcare. by examining common patterns of misclassification, researchers and clinicians can refine model accuracy, improve transparency, and reduce risks in clinical decision - making. the errors often arise due to issues such as data imbalance, overlapping features, poor data quality, insufficient training samples, and biases within the training data. in healthcare, misclassification can have serious repercussions - false positives may lead to unnecessary treatments, false negatives can result in missed diagnoses, and both undermine trust in ai systems, raising ethical and legal concerns.

records.text: there are several factors and challenges that limit the utility of brain tumor imaging datasets : • limited data availability : many studies rely on small datasets, leading to potential overfitting and limited generalizability [ 99 ]. medical imaging datasets are typically smaller than those in general computer vision due to privacy concerns, acquisition costs, and the need for expert annotations. this limitation is particularly pronounced for rare tumor types. while data augmentation and transfer learning partially address this issue, they cannot fully compensate for the diversity of real - world cases. regarding the limited size e. g., most public datasets contain fewer than 1, 000 cases, insufficient for optimal dl performance. so, in many domains - especially medical imaging - datasets are small due to privacy issues, high acquisition costs, limited patient populations, and difficulties in sharing across institutions. • data heterogeneity : data collected from different institutions, scanners, imaging protocols, or patient populations vary significantly. for example, mri scans may differ in intensity distribution, contrast, and orientation. scanner and protocol variations produce significant data heterogeneity. variations in acquisition protocols, differences in scanners, image quality, and institutional practices introduce significant heterogeneity [ 100 ]. • class imbalance : some classes ( e. g., healthy controls ) dominate the dataset, while others ( rare diseases, earlystage conditions ) are underrepresented. uneven distribution of tumor types in datasets can bias model training towards more prevalent classes [ 101 ]. limited availability of annotated brain tumor imaging data remains a primary challenge. rare tumor types are often underrepresented, leading to class imbalance issues. brain tumors exhibit significant class imbalance, both in terms of tumor types ( with some being much rarer than others ) and segmentation regions ( with enhancing tumor typically occupying a small fraction of the brain volume ).

• integration with clinical workflow : integrating ai models into clinical workflows presents logistical and technical challenges. deployment of dl models requires seamless integration with existing clinical workflows and picture archiving and communication systems ( pacs ). technical barriers include compatibility issues, computational requirements, the need for real - time processing, and alert fatigue from automated findings. there are several successful integration

include : containerization, edge computing, and hybrid cloud - edge architectures. embedding ai systems into existing clinical workflows without disrupting efficiency remains challenging [ 105 ]. • regulatory approval : ai - based medical devices require regulatory approval ( e. g., fda clearance ), involving extensive validation and documentation. the dynamic nature of deep learning models, which may be continuously updated with new data, poses challenges for traditional regulatory frameworks. regulatory approval pathways for ai in neuroimaging remain evolving and complex. there are challenges of regulatory considerations include : clinical validation requirements, software - as - a - medical - device ( samd ) classification, continuous learning system regulation, and responsibility allocation for ai - assisted decisions. obtaining necessary regulatory clearances for clinical deployment is a complex and time - consuming process [ 106 ]. • clinician acceptance : building trust among clinicians requires transparent and explainable ai systems [ 107 ]. • real - time processing : clinical decision - making often requires real - time or near - real - time processing capabilities [ 108 ]. • prospective validation : most dl models for brain tumor analysis have been evaluated retrospectively on curated datasets. prospective validation in clinical settings, with diverse patient populations and real - world scenarios, is essential but still limited in the literature.

• model complexity vs. interpretability : more complex models often achieve higher accuracy but at the expense of interpretability, which is crucial in clinical settings [ 109 ]. • overfitting : especially problematic with small datasets, limiting the model ' s generalization ability [ 110 ]. • computational requirements : advanced 3d models and multi - modal approaches demand substantial computational resources [ 111 ]. • domain shift : models trained on data from one institution often perform poorly when applied to data from different institutions due to variations in imaging protocols [ 112 ].

• limited representation capacity : hand - crafted features may not capture the full complexity and heterogeneity of brain tumors [ 114 ]. • curse of dimensionality : high - dimensional feature spaces with limited samples lead to statistical challenges [ 115 ].

• black - box nature : limited interpretability hampers clinical acceptance and validation [ 116 ]. • data dependency : performance heavily relies on the quality and quantity of training data [ 117 ]. • generalization issues : models often struggle to generalize across different scanners, protocols, and patient populations [ 118 ]. • uncertainty quantification : many dl approaches lack reliable methods for uncertainty estimation, which is crucial for clinical decision - making [ 119 ].

most publicly available datasets suffer from demographic and geographic biases : • age distribution : many datasets, such as brats, are skewed toward older patients, underrepresenting pediatric brain tumors with different characteristics. • ethnic representation : limited diversity in patient populations, with most datasets collected in north america and europe. • socioeconomic factors : datasets predominantly from well - resourced medical centers, potentially biasing models toward high - quality imaging available in such settings.

dl models trained on one dataset often generalize poorly to images acquired with different scanners, field strengths, or protocols. this domain shift is a major barrier to clinical translation. approaches like gan - based domain adaptation and domain - adversarial training [ 120 ] have shown promise but are still evolving.

dl models, especially the cnns, often function as " black boxes, " making their decisions difficult to interpret and limiting clinical trust and adoption. in clinical settings, interpretability is essential to build trust and facilitate adoption.
